title: Big tech, law enforcement make final pitches as Senate considers data access bill's future
summary: Big tech is launching its final salvo to scale back the Liberal government's contentious proposed national security legislation, which would change how companies retain and hand over user data to…

image.caption: Bill C-22 would give law enforcement agencies and CSIS faster access to electronic information, such as messages sent via cellphone, during investigations. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Big tech is launching its final salvo to scale back the Liberal government's contentious proposed national security legislation, which would change how companies retain and hand over user data to Canadian police and intelligence officers, as it nears its last legislative hurdle in the Senate. Law enforcement agencies are also making a passionate appeal for senators to pass the bill as soon as possible.
Senators will soon decide if lawful access legislation needs further amending

Big tech is launching its final salvo to scale back the Liberal government's contentious proposed national security legislation, which would change how companies retain and hand over user data to Canadian police and intelligence officers, as it nears its last legislative hurdle in the Senate.
The lawful access legislation, Bill C-22, is before a Senate committee again on Monday before it goes through clause-by-clause consideration Tuesday.

The bill would give law enforcement agencies and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) faster access to electronic information during investigations — something the community has warned is essential for public safety in an age where most evidence has a digital trail.
One of the most controversial parts of the bill would compel tech companies to adapt their systems to preserve and turn over information to investigators if they have a warrant.

Following months of backlash, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree brought in amendments. But the Senate has heard over the last month that those changes don't go far enough to satisfy privacy advocates and some of the world's biggest tech companies.

Meta would 'consider' pulling services if bill passes as is

blocks.text: If the bill passes without further amendments, electronic service providers wouldn't be compelled to decrypt information unless they supplied the encryption and hold the key, which the federal government argues would more closely align with U.S. law.
The changes also limit how long providers must hold on to metadata from one year to six months.

But the bill still gives the minister the authority to issue confidential ministerial orders to electronic service providers. The secrecy provision has rankled companies who argue they wouldn't be able to push back if they have concerns.
Critics insist the amended legislation doesn't go far enough, leaving users' encrypted information vulnerable to malicious actors and creating a surveillance state.
Meta would consider pulling apps from Canada over 'lawful access' bill
On Monday, the Senate's national security committee will hear from Google and Apple officials who continue to push for further changes.

In its submission to the committee, Apple said tools given to police to protect Canadians "must not come at the expense of the security and privacy protections on which Canadians depend to protect their fundamental rights, their economic prosperity or the security of the nation."
Google wrote in its submission that the bill could enable the government to require providers to change their products to create new surveillance capabilities on behalf of law enforcement.

"Public transparency is critical for the effective functioning of a democratic state, particularly in the context of state surveillance. If surveillance directives are made in secret, citizens cannot understand or scrutinize state power," it reads.
Companies threatening to withdraw from Canada
Some companies are threatening to withdraw services if C-22 receives royal assent in its current form.
Signal, a popular encrypted messaging app, threatened to pull out of Canada if the bill passes as written.

Last week, representatives from Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and the encrypted messaging app WhatsApp, argued the Canadian government is "imposing a law that it is not technically feasible to comply with and still offer secure, end-to-end encrypted services to Canadians."

blocks.text: When asked if the legislation would mean the company would pull some of its services from Canada, Meta's head of public policy for Canada Rachel Curran said the company would have to "review all of our options."
But she said it is something the company would have to "consider."

Apple removed its strongest data security tool for U.K. customers last year after the British government asked the company to bypass encryption to access customer data. The company has challenged the order in a case still before the courts.

Officials with Apple, speaking to reporters on the condition they not be named, have said repeatedly they don't want to remove their advanced data protection service from Canadian devices, but reiterated that the company will never build what it sees as a back door.
Law enforcement argues Canada falling behind

Law enforcement and child protection agencies have made passionate appeals before the Senate committee to pass the bill without delay. The government first introduced lawful access legislation in June 2025 as part of its Strong Borders Act, before it was split into separate bills following opposition.

"To be blunt, our society is losing the effort to combat the exploitation of children over the internet," Andrew Ullock, chair of the Ontario Child Sexual Exploitation Investigators Association and a detective with Peel Regional Police testified last week.

Ullock and other witnesses, including from the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, the Canadian Police Association and the National Police Federation, argued police are outpaced by criminals and extremists online and need updated laws to close that gap.
Tech giants 'misinterpreting' lawful access safeguards: public safety minister

Ontario Provincial Police Commissioner Thomas Carrique said, in practical terms, Bill C-22 would help police avoid wasting "valuable time" by helping quickly pinpoint the right service provider and help address lengthy delays when critical evidence is held outside of Canada "and at risk of disappearing."
"Canadians have a right to privacy. They also have a right to safety, to justice and to expect that lawful judicial orders can be effective when serious crimes are committed against them," he said.
Lloyd Richardson, the director of technology at the Canadian Centre for Child Protection, called big tech's threats to retreat from Canada "a big bluff."
"I think everyone in this room knows that WhatsApp is not going to disappear from Canada if this legislation passed as is," Richardson told the committee last week.
If the Senate puts forward amendments, the bill would be sent back to the House of Commons, where the Liberals hold a majority.
